claim: RNF10 was identified as a binding partner for GluN2A through yeast two-hybrid screening using the GluN2A C-terminal domain (aa 839-1461) as bait.
source: In order to identify new binding partners for GluN2A, we performed a yeast two-hybrid screening using the C-terminal domain (aa 839–1461, without the aa 1462–1464 PDZ-binding sequence) as bait. We obtained a number of positive clones including RNF10 (Seki et al., 2000; Hoshikawa et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental method (yeast two-hybrid screening) used to identify RNF10 as a GluN2A binding partner.

claim: RNF10 is expressed in both glial and neuronal cells.
source: Using specific glial (GFAP) and neuronal (MAP2) markers, we confirmed that RNF10 is expressed in both glia (Figure 1A) and neurons (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A and 1B using cell-type specific markers.

claim: In neurons, RNF10 displays a nuclear and somatodendritic distribution.
source: Interestingly, in neurons RNF10 displayed a nuclear and somatodendritic distribution (Figure 1B).
evidence: The subcellular localization is demonstrated by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 1B.

claim: Transfected GFP-RNF10 co-localizes with PSD-95 and GluN2A at dendritic spines of hippocampal neurons.
source: Moreover, transfected GFP-RNF10 displayed a prominent co-localization with PSD-95 and GluN2A at the dendritic spines of hippocampal neurons (Figure 1C).
evidence: Co-localization is demonstrated by confocal microscopy in Figure 1C.

claim: Endogenous RNF10 shows clustered immunolabeling along dendrites that co-localizes with GluN2A and PSD-95.
source: Similarly, analysis of endogenous RNF10 in DIV14 primary hippocampal neurons showed clustered RNF10 immunolabeling along dendrites and most puncta co-localized with GluN2A (Figure 1D, left panels) and PSD-95 (Figure 1D, right panels).
evidence: Endogenous protein localization is shown by immunofluorescence in Figure 1D.

claim: RNF10 is associated with synaptic fractions and is prominently present in PSD fractions.
source: Subcellular fractionation demonstrated that RNF10 is associated with synaptic fractions and that it is prominently present in PSD fractions (Figure 1E).
evidence: Biochemical fractionation data is shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In the CA1 region of adult rat hippocampus, RNF10 shows intense signal in soma and nuclei together with punctate staining along MAP2-positive dendrites.
source: Finally, immunofluorescence analysis of the CA1 region of the adult rat hippocampus revealed the presence of an intense signal for RNF10 in the soma and nuclei together with a punctate staining along MAP2-positive dendrites (Figure 1F).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data from adult tissue is shown in Figure 1F.

claim: GluN2A silencing in primary hippocampal neurons induces a significant decrease in RNF10 synaptic levels.
source: Interestingly, GluN2A silencing in primary hippocampal neurons (Figure 1G) induced a significant decrease in RNF10 synaptic levels, as indicated by the reduction of RNF10 co-localization with PSD-95 (Figure 1H).
evidence: The effect of GluN2A knockdown on RNF10 localization is demonstrated in Figures 1G and 1H.

claim: RNF10 specifically interacts with GluN2A but not with GluN2B subunit of NMDARs.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation (co-i.p.) studies performed from hippocampal P2 crude membrane fractions indicated a specific interaction of RNF10 with GluN2A but not with GluN2B subunit of the NMDARs (Figure 2A).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments demonstrate selective interaction with GluN2A in Figure 2A.

claim: Jacob preferentially co-immunoprecipitates with GluN2B from rat brain homogenate.
source: Indeed, the affinity-purified pan-Jacob antibody preferentially co-i.p. GluN2B from rat brain homogenate. Only a very faint band of GluN2A was detected in the complex with Jacob (Figure 2B), which might potentially represent synaptic tri-heteromeric GluN1/GluN2A/GluN2B NMDARs.
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data for Jacob is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In COS-7 cells, RNF10 co-immunoprecipitates with GluN2A but not GluN2B.
source: In addition, cell lysates from COS-7 cells transfected with HA-GluN1 and GFP-GluN2A or GFP-GluN2B constructs were immunoprecipitated with anti-RNF10 and immunoblotted for GFP. The results confirmed that GluN2A interacts with RNF10, whereas GluN2B failed to associate with RNF10 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Heterologous expression and co-immunoprecipitation data is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In COS-7 cells, RNF10 shows high co-localization with GluN2A (73.8% ± 2.9%) but not with GluN2B (31.3% ± 1.7%).
source: Immunofluorescence studies revealed the presence of RNF10 aggregates with a high co-localization degree with GluN2A but not with GluN2B (Figure 2D; 73.8% ± 2.9% GluN2A/RNF10 vs 31.3.% ± 1.7% GluN2B/RNF10; p<0.001, n=15; unpaired Student's t-test).
evidence: Quantitative co-localization data from immunofluorescence is provided with statistical analysis.

claim: RNF10 and GluN2A are in close proximity (<40 nm) at synapses as demonstrated by proximity ligation assay.
source: Finally, RNF10 clustering with GluN2A at synapses was confirmed by proximity ligation assay (PLA). As shown in Figure 2E, a large number of PLA signals were detected when the two antibodies RNF10 and GluN2A were used indicating these two proteins are in close proximity (<40 nm) to each other.
evidence: Proximity ligation assay data is shown in Figure 2E demonstrating close molecular proximity.

claim: Transfection of COS-7 cells with GluN2A but not GluN2B induces redistribution of endogenous RNF10 from nucleus to cytoplasm.
source: Notably, transfection of COS-7 cells with GluN2A but not GluN2B induces a highly significant redistribution of endogenous RNF10 from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, thus suggesting that GluN2A traps RNF10 outside the nucleus (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: Subcellular redistribution is demonstrated by immunofluorescence in Figures 2F-G.

claim: RNF10 interacts with the GluN2A juxta-membrane region (aa 991-1049).
source: The pull-down assay performed from adult rat brain tissue using glutathione S-transferase (GST)-GluN2A C-terminal domain fusion proteins (Figure 3A) revealed that RNF10 interacts with the GluN2A cytoplasmic tail (CT; aa 839–1464) but failed to bind the distal part of the GluN2A C-terminus (aa 1049–1464) (Figure 3B, upper panel). In addition, GluN2A(839–991) failed to interact with RNF10 (Figure 3B, lower panel), thus indicating GluN2A(991–1049) is needed for the formation of the GluN2A/RNF10 complex.
evidence: Pull-down assays with deletion constructs map the binding region in Figure 3A-B.

claim: The presence of free Ca2+ (2 mM) significantly reduces GluN2A binding to GST-RNF10.
source: Using a pull-down assay we found that the presence of free Ca2+ (2 mM) in the buffer significantly reduced GluN2A binding to GST-RNF10 FL (Figure 3E; -37.8% ± 6.2%; p<0.01).
evidence: Pull-down assay with calcium demonstrates calcium-dependent regulation in Figure 3E.

claim: Ca2+/CaM completely prevents the interaction between RNF10 and GluN2A in pull-down assays.
source: In addition, co-incubation with exogenous CaM completely prevented the interaction between RNF10 and GluN2A in the pull-down assay (Figure 3G) only in the presence of Ca2+ in the buffer (Bajaj et al., 2014).
evidence: Pull-down assay with calcium and calmodulin is shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The RNF10 N-terminal region (aa 1-221) is crucial for binding to GluN2A.
source: Finally, pull-down assay performed from adult rat brain tissue using GST-RNF10 fusion proteins confirmed that the RNF10 N-terminal region 1–221 is crucial for the binding to GluN2A (Figure 3M).
evidence: Pull-down assays with RNF10 deletion constructs map the binding domain in Figure 3M.

claim: RNF10 silencing produces a significant reduction in dendritic spine density.
source: In particular, RNF10 silencing produced a significant reduction in dendritic spine density (Figure 4B) without any effect on dendritic spine length (Figure 4C) or dendritic spine head width (Figure 4D).
evidence: Morphological analysis of dendritic spines after RNF10 knockdown is shown in Figure 4B-D.

claim: The effect of RNF10 silencing on dendritic spine density is fully rescued by co-expressing a wild-type human variant of RNF10 resistant to shRNA.
source: Notably, the effect of RNF10 silencing on dendritic spine density was fully rescued by co-expressing a wild-type human variant of RNF10 resistant to shRNA (see Materials and methods; flag-RNF10; Figure 4A–E).
evidence: Rescue experiment demonstrates specificity of the knockdown effect in Figures 4A-E.

claim: RNF10 silencing results in a significant decrease of GluN2A, PSD-95, and GluA1 protein levels in dissociated neurons and organotypic slices.
source: Most importantly, RNF10 silencing resulted in a significant decrease of GluN2A, PSD-95 and the GluA1 subunit of the AMPA receptor (AMPAR) protein levels in the total cell homogenate of pLKO-shRNF10-infected dissociated neurons and organotypic slices (Figure 4F).
evidence: Western blot analysis of synaptic proteins after RNF10 knockdown is shown in Figure 4F.

claim: RNF10 silencing modulates the expression of genes involved in excitatory synaptic transmission and dendritic spine morphology.
source: Interestingly, heat map of differentially expressed genes (Figure 5A), gene ontology analysis (Figure 5B) and real-time PCR validation (Figure 4G) showed that RNF10 silencing modulated the expression of several genes involved in excitatory synaptic transmission and dendritic spine morphology (Vogt et al., 2007; Michaluk et al., 2011; Ramakers et al., 2012).
evidence: Microarray and qPCR data demonstrate transcriptional changes in Figures 4G and 5A-B, supported by citations.

claim: Enhanced excitatory activity with Bicuculline and 4-AP significantly decreases RNF10 immunoreactivity along dendrites.
source: Enhanced excitatory activity significantly decreased RNF10 immunoreactivity along dendrites as compared to untreated neurons, without affecting PSD-95 (Figure 6A) labeling and induced a significant increase in RNF10 nuclear staining (Figure 6D, left panels).
evidence: Immunofluorescence analysis after neuronal stimulation is shown in Figures 6A and 6D.

claim: Bicuculline treatment induces RNF10-tdEOS translocation from distal dendrites to the nucleus.
source: Bic treatment induced a significant increase in RNF10-tdEOS photoconverted fluorescence intensity in the nucleus compared to untreated neurons accompanied by a decline in distal dendrites (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging of photoconverted RNF10 demonstrates long-distance transport in Figures 6B-C.

claim: Co-incubation of Bicuculline with the GluN2A-specific inhibitor NVP-AAM007 significantly reduces RNF10 nuclear accumulation.
source: Interestingly, the co-incubation of Bic with the GluN2A-specific inhibitor NVP-AAM007 (NVP, 50 nM or 300 nM) led to a significant reduction of RNF10 nuclear accumulation compared to Bic treatment alone also at a concentration of 50 nM, which is known to preferentially block di-heteromeric GluN1/GluN2A and not tri-heteromeric GluN1/GluN2A/GluN2B NMDARs (Figure 6D; Foster et al., 2010).
evidence: Pharmacological inhibition experiments are shown in Figure 6D with citation support.

claim: Synaptic NMDAR stimulation induces a significant increase in RNF10 nuclear accumulation.
source: Synaptic NMDARs stimulation induced a significant increase in RNF10 nuclear accumulation (Figure 6E, left panels).
evidence: Selective synaptic stimulation protocol results are shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Extrasynaptic NMDAR activation fails to induce translocation of RNF10 from dendrites to the nucleus.
source: On the other hand, two different protocols known to activate extrasynaptic NMDARs (Hardingham et al., 2002; Karpova et al., 2013) failed to induce the translocation of RNF10 from dendrites to the nucleus (Figure 6E, right panel).
evidence: Extrasynaptic stimulation protocols are shown in Figure 6E with citation support.

claim: Jacob dissociates from synapses following activation of GluN2B but not di-heteromeric GluN2A containing NMDARs.
source: This increase was abolished in the presence of the GluN2B antagonist ifenprodil (5 µM), but not with GluN2A antagonist NVP-AAM077 (50 nM) indicating that Jacob dissociates from the synapses following activation of GluN2B but not di-heteromeric GluN2A containing NMDAR (Figure 6F).
evidence: Pharmacological experiments with Jacob are shown in Figure 6F.

claim: RNF10 contains two putative nuclear localization sequences (NLS1: aa 591-599; NLS2: aa 784-791).
source: Analysis of the RNF10 sequence showed the presence of two putative NLS motifs (NLS1: aa 591–599; NLS2: aa 784–791; Seki et al., 2000; Marfori et al., 2011).
evidence: Sequence analysis identifies NLS motifs with citation support.

claim: RNF10 truncated mutants lacking one or both NLS motifs fail to localize to the nucleus in primary hippocampal neurons.
source: Myc-RNF10 FL showed an intense nuclear accumulation (as the endogenous protein; Figure 7A). However, both truncated mutants failed to localize to the nucleus as indicated by a very low co-localization with the nuclear marker Dapi (Figure 7A).
evidence: Localization of deletion mutants is shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Overexpression of Myc-RNF10 (1-611) construct produces a significant reduction in the density of PSD-95-positive puncta along dendrites.
source: Notably, the overexpression of Myc-RNF10 (1–611) construct produced a significant reduction in the density of PSD-95-positive puncta along dendrites (Figure 7B, upper panels) similar to that observed following RNF10 silencing (Figure 7B, lower panels), indicating that this protein fragment can act in a dominant negative manner.
evidence: Dominant negative effect is demonstrated in Figure 7B.

claim: RNF10 co-localizes with importin α1 and surface GluN2A along dendrites of hippocampal neurons.
source: RNF10 displayed a prominent co-localization with importin α1 (KPNA2 gene product; see Zienkiewicz et al., 2013) and surface GluN2A along dendrites of DIV14 primary hippocampal neurons (Figure 7C).
evidence: Co-localization is shown by immunofluorescence in Figure 7C with citation.

claim: Importin α1 is present in purified PSDs from rat hippocampus.
source: In agreement with previous data about other importins (Thompson et al., 2004; Jeffrey et al., 2009; Marfori et al., 2011; Ch'ng et al., 2012), analysis of importin α1 subcellular distribution showed its presence in purified PSDs from rat hippocampus (Figure 7D).
evidence: Biochemical fractionation data is shown in Figure 7D with citation support.

claim: RNF10 interacts with importin α1 in neuronal cells.
source: Immunoprecipitation experiments performed revealed that RNF10 interacts with importin α1 in neuronal cells (Figure 7E, upper panel).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data is shown in Figure 7E.

claim: RNF10 co-precipitation with importin α1 is more prominent in PSDs than in homogenate fraction.
source: Interestingly, RNF10 co-precipitation with importin α1 was detected both in PSD and homogenate fraction but it was much more prominent in PSDs (Figure 7E, lower panel).
evidence: Differential co-immunoprecipitation from subcellular fractions is shown in Figure 7E.

claim: RNF10 can interact with majority of importin α isoforms except importin α3 (KPNA4 gene product).
source: As shown in Figure 7F, RNF10 can interact with majority of importin α isoforms except importin α3 (KPNA4 gene product).
evidence: Heterologous co-immunoprecipitation with multiple importin isoforms is shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Bicuculline treatment significantly increases RNF10/importin α1 association.
source: Bic treatment significantly increased RNF10/importin α1 association (Figure 7G).
evidence: Activity-dependent change in protein interaction is shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Bicuculline treatment significantly increases RNF10 interaction with transcription factor Meox2.
source: Interestingly, also the RNF10 interaction with the transcription factor Meox2 was significantly increased by Bic treatment (Figure 7H).
evidence: Activity-dependent change in protein interaction is shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Bicuculline treatment significantly decreases RNF10/GluN2A interaction.
source: On the contrary, Bic treatment significantly decreased RNF10/GluN2A interaction compared to control neurons (Figure 7H), which is in agreement with the reduction of RNF10 labeling along dendrites (see Figure 6A).
evidence: Activity-dependent change in protein interaction is shown in Figure 7H.

claim: High-frequency field stimulation (18s@50Hz) induces a significant increase in RNF10-tdEOS photoconverted fluorescence intensity in the nucleus.
source: We observed a significant increase in RNF10-tdEOS photoconverted green-to-red fluorescence intensity in the nucleus when compared to unstimulated neurons (Figure 8B,C) accompanied by a concomitant decline in distal dendrites upon stimulation (Figure 8C, lower panels).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging after LTP induction is shown in Figures 8B-C.

claim: Chemical LTP induction leads to a significant decrease in endogenous RNF10 immunostaining along dendrites.
source: Under these experimental conditions, cLTP induction produced a significant decrease in endogenous RNF10 immunostaining along dendrites (Figure 8D) and a concomitant significant increase of RNF10 localization in the nucleus as revealed by western blotting in a crude nuclear fraction (Figure 8G) and co-localization assays with the nuclear marker Dapi (Figure 8F and Figure 9B).
evidence: Immunofluorescence and biochemical data after cLTP are shown in Figures 8D, 8F, 8G, and 9B.

claim: Chemical LTP detaches RNF10 from GluN2A.
source: Consistent with the above-described results (see Figure 7H), cLTP detached RNF10 from GluN2A (Figure 8E).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation after cLTP is shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Anisomycin treatment does not prevent nuclear accumulation of RNF10 following cLTP.
source: Finally, we used anisomycin to exclude the possibility that de novo RNF10 protein synthesis could account for the nuclear accumulation of RNF10 following cLTP (Figure 8F,G). Anisomycin treatment did not prevent nuclear accumulation of RNF10 in this assay (Figure 8F,G).
evidence: Protein synthesis inhibition experiments are shown in Figures 8F-G.

claim: NLS2 peptide induces a significant reduction of RNF10/importin α1 interaction.
source: Notably, NLS2 peptide induced a significant reduction of RNF10/importin α1 interaction when compared to treatment with TAT (used as control peptide; Figure 9B).
evidence: Peptide competition experiment is shown in Figure 9B.

claim: NLS2 peptide completely prevents the LTP-dependent increase in nuclear RNF10.
source: The NLS2 peptide completely prevented the LTP-dependent increase in nuclear RNF10, as indicated by immunofluorescence (Figure 9C,D) and by immunoblot analyses of RNF10 protein levels in a P1 crude nuclear fraction (Figure 9G,H).
evidence: Peptide inhibition of nuclear translocation is shown in Figures 9C-D and 9G-H.

claim: NLS2 peptide treatment prevents the decrease in dendritic RNF10 labeling observed after induction of cLTP.
source: Importantly, treatment with NLS2 peptide also prevented the decrease in dendritic RNF10 labeling observed after induction of cLTP (Figure 9E,F).
evidence: Peptide effect on dendritic RNF10 is shown in Figures 9E-F.

claim: Induction of chemical long-term depression (cLTD) does not modify RNF10 binding to GluN2A.
source: Conversely, induction of chemical long-term depression (cLTD) did not modify RNF10 binding to GluN2A (Figure 9I; +0.9% ± 4.8%, cLTD vs. control; p>0.05) and the nuclear distribution of RNF10 in hippocampal neurons (Figure 9J).
evidence: cLTD experiments are shown in Figures 9I-J with quantification.

claim: Bicuculline treatment increases p21WAF1/cip1 protein levels.
source: Bic treatment increased p21WAF1/cip1 levels as evaluated by immunofluorescence (Figure 10A,B) and Western blot analysis (Figure 10C).
evidence: Immunofluorescence and Western blot data are shown in Figures 10A-C.

claim: Up-regulation of p21WAF1/cip1 by Bicuculline is significantly attenuated by co-treatment with MK801.
source: Up-regulation of p21WAF1/cip1 was significantly attenuated by co-treatment with the NMDAR blocker MK801 (Figure 10A–C).
evidence: Pharmacological inhibition experiments are shown in Figures 10A-C.

claim: The increase in p21WAF1/cip1 protein levels following stimulation of synaptic NMDARs is completely prevented by RNF10 silencing.
source: Notably, the increase in p21WAF1/cip1 protein levels following stimulation of synaptic NMDARs was completely prevented by RNF10 silencing (Figure 10E), indicating that modulation of p21WAF1/cip1 expression is RNF10-dependent.
evidence: RNF10 knockdown effect on target gene expression is shown in Figure 10E.

claim: Chemical LTP increases p21WAF1/cip1 expression in an RNF10-dependent manner.
source: In addition, the same effect on p21WAF1/cip1 levels was observed following induction of cLTP. Again, the increased expression of p21WAF1/cip1 was prevented by RNF10 silencing (Figure 10F).
evidence: cLTP effect on target gene expression and RNF10 dependence is shown in Figure 10F.

claim: RNF10 silencing decreases the expression of Ophn1 after synaptic stimulation.
source: Finally, RNF10 silencing decreased the expression of the newly identified RNF10 target gene Ophn1 (see Figure 4G,H) also after synaptic stimulation (Figure 10G).
evidence: Effect on Ophn1 expression is shown in Figure 10G.

claim: Down-regulation of RNF10 leads to a significant decrease of mEPSC frequency but not amplitude in basal conditions.
source: In basal conditions, down-regulation of RNF10 led to a significant decrease of the frequency (Figure 11A,C) but not the amplitude (Figure 11A,B) of mEPSCs.
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings are shown in Figures 11A-C.

claim: RNF10 silencing prevents the long-lasting increase of mEPSC amplitude and frequency induced by cLTP.
source: Furthermore, while in control neurons cLTP induction resulted in a long-lasting increase of the amplitude and frequency of mEPSCs, this effect was totally prevented in neurons transfected with shRNF10 (Figure 11D,E).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings after cLTP are shown in Figures 11D-E.

claim: Co-transfection of FlagRNF10 fully rescues the physiological long-lasting increase of mEPSC amplitude and frequency.
source: Again, co-transfection of FlagRNF10 fully rescued a physiological long-lasting increase of the amplitude (Figure 11D) and frequency (Figure 11E) of mEPSCs.
evidence: Rescue experiments are shown in Figures 11D-E.

claim: RNF10 overexpression increases PSD-95 cluster width in absence of stimulation and occludes further increase following cLTP induction.
source: RNF10 overexpression produced an increase in PSD-95 clusters width also in absence of stimulation and occluding any further increase of PSD-95 clusters width following induction of cLTP (Figure 11F).
evidence: Morphological analysis after RNF10 overexpression is shown in Figure 11F.

claim: RNF10 silencing blocks cLTP-dependent modification of PSD-95 clusters.
source: On the other hand, RNF10 silencing blocked any cLTP-dependent modification of PSD-95 clusters (Figure 11G).
evidence: Morphological analysis after RNF10 knockdown is shown in Figure 11G.

claim: RNF10 silencing precludes any increase in GluA1 cluster width induced by cLTP.
source: Evaluation of GluA1 synaptic cluster size confirmed that RNF10 silencing precludes any increase in GluA1 clusters width induced by cLTP (Figure 11I).
evidence: Morphological analysis of GluA1 clusters is shown in Figure 11I.

claim: RNF10 is a novel synaptonuclear protein messenger that specifically links activation of synaptic GluN2A-containing NMDARs to nuclear gene expression.
source: This report describes a novel synapse-to-nucleus signaling pathway that specifically links activation of synaptic GluN2A-containing NMDARs to nuclear gene expression.
evidence: This is a summary claim stated in the Discussion section integrating multiple experimental findings.

claim: RNF10 dissociates from the NMDAR complex in an activity-dependent manner.
source: RNF10 dissociates from the NMDAR complex in an activity-dependent manner and we provide compelling evidence for the importin-dependent long-distance transport from synapto-dendritic compartments to the nucleus.
evidence: This is a summary claim stated in the Discussion section integrating multiple experimental findings.

claim: RNF10 and CaM share the same GluN2A binding region (aa 991-1029).
source: Among others, RNF10 and CaM share the same GluN2A binding region (aa 991–1029; Bajaj et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is based on mapping data and cited literature.

claim: RNF10 binding to GluN2A plays a key role for RNF10 anchoring at the excitatory synapse.
source: Overall, our data show that RNF10 binding to GluN2A plays a key role for RNF10 anchoring at the excitatory synapse but also interfere with the formation of CaM/NMDAR complex.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim in the Discussion based on experimental data.

claim: The presence of RNF10 in close proximity to the receptor channel allows for rapid calcium-dependent dissociation of RNF10/GluN2A complex following NMDAR activation.
source: Moreover, the presence of RNF10 in close proximity to the receptor channel allows for a rapid calcium-dependent dissociation of RNF10/GluN2A complex following NMDAR activation and for the subsequent formation of RNF10/importin complex.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation in the Discussion based on experimental findings.

claim: Interaction of RNF10 with importin α1 represents a key step for its nuclear translocation.
source: Here, we show that interaction of RNF10 with importin α1 represents a key step for its nuclear translocation.
evidence: This is a summary claim in the Discussion based on multiple experiments.

claim: Synaptonuclear trafficking of RNF10 is involved in the control of gene expression necessary for LTP-type synaptic plasticity in hippocampal neurons.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that synaptonuclear trafficking of RNF10 is involved in the control of gene expression, which is necessary for LTP-type synaptic plasticity in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim in the Discussion integrating multiple experimental findings.

claim: RNF10 acts as a positive regulator of neuronal differentiation.
source: A very recent study performed in P19 carcinoma cell line and in mouse cerebellar granule cells suggests that RNF10 acts as a positive regulator of neuronal differentiation, as its knockdown reduced the number of cells expressing early and late neuronal markers (Malik et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature.

claim: RNF10 target genes include MMP9, Arhgef6, ArhGap4, and Ophn1, which are known to be involved in regulation of excitatory synapse function and morphology.
source: Notably, microarray, subsequent real-time PCR and western blotting analysis allowed us to find, among others, novel RNF10 target genes known to be involved in the regulation of the excitatory synapse function and morphology (Vogt et al., 2007; Michaluk et al., 2011; Bagni et al., 2012; Ramakers et al., 2012; Pavlowsky et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on microarray data and cited literature.

claim: RNF10 target genes (MMP9, Arhgef6, ArhGap4, Ophn1) are mutated or dysregulated in intellectual disability syndromes.
source: Intriguingly, all these genes are mutated or dysregulated in intellectual disability syndromes in humans and/or in the corresponding mouse models (Vogt et al., 2007; Michaluk et al., 2011; Ramakers et al., 2012), which are characterized by various alterations in dendritic spines, thus suggesting a key role in synaptic effects observed following RNF10 silencing.
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature and inference.

claim: An impaired RNF10-mediated synaptonuclear signaling is responsible for the reduction of dendritic spine density observed following RNF10 silencing.
source: This result strongly indicates that an impaired RNF10-mediated synaptonuclear signaling and not a reduction of RNF10 synaptic levels is responsible for the reduction of dendritic spine density observed following RNF10 silencing.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim in the Discussion based on dominant negative experiments.

claim: Activation of synaptic NMDARs promotes the expression of synaptic plasticity-related genes.
source: In general, activation of synaptic NMDARs promotes the expression of synaptic plasticity-related genes, whereas activation of extrasynaptic NMDARs has been correlated to CNS pathological conditions (Hardingham and Bading, 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature and established knowledge.

claim: Jacob can encode and transduce the synaptic and extrasynaptic origin of GluN2B NMDAR signals to the nucleus.
source: The protein messenger Jacob, following long-distance transport and nuclear import, can encode and transduce the synaptic and extrasynaptic origin of GluN2B NMDAR signals to the nucleus and might dock a NMDA-receptor-derived signalosome to nuclear target sites in a stimulus-dependent manner (Karpova et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature.

claim: Activation of synaptic but not extrasynaptic NMDARs leads to an increase in RNF10 nuclear localization.
source: Notably, here we show that activation of synaptic but not extrasynaptic NMDARs leads to an increase in RNF10 nuclear localization.
evidence: This is a summary claim in the Discussion based on experimental data.

claim: RNF10 moves to the nucleus after induction of LTP but not LTD.
source: Similarly to what was previously described for Jacob (Behnisch et al., 2011), we observe that RNF10 moves to the nucleus after induction of LTP but not LTD, modulating the expression of Meox2 target genes.
evidence: This is a summary claim in the Discussion based on experimental data and cited literature.

claim: Inhibition of GluN2A- but not GluN2B-containing NMDARs is sufficient to block RNF10 trafficking to the nucleus.
source: However, in contrast to Jacob, inhibition of GluN2A- but not GluN2B-containing NMDARs is sufficient to block RNF10 trafficking to the nucleus, its interaction with the transcription factor Meox2 and the expression of the Meox2 target gene p21WAF1/cip1.
evidence: This is a summary claim in the Discussion based on pharmacological experiments.

claim: Synapse-to-nucleus protein transport provides specific ways to inform the nucleus about different types of synaptic activity.
source: Overall our data together with the findings from other recent reports (Kaushik et al., 2014; Rishal and Fainzilber, 2014; Panayotis et al., 2015), suggest that synapse-to-nucleus protein transport provide specific ways to inform the nucleus about very different types of synaptic activity.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim in the Discussion based on data and cited literature.

claim: RNF10 represents a novel synaptonuclear protein messenger responsible for long-lasting re-shaping of dendritic spines required for postsynaptic modifications needed to convey LTP induction.
source: In this context, RNF10 represents a novel synaptonuclear protein messenger responsible for long-lasting re-shaping of dendritic spines as observed after specific synaptic stimuli and required for postsynaptic modifications needed to convey LTP induction.
evidence: This is a concluding interpretive claim in the Discussion integrating all findings.
